catalog_quote: In Bidayuh the ultima (last syllable) is the nucleus of the word. It receives the peak of word stress—at least in citation forms (words that are pronounced individually). [...] In some words of the shape (C)V.V(C), in western dialects (Singai, Jagoi) and also in Rara, the same vowel occurs in both the ultima (last syllable) and the penult (second-to-last syllable). In such words initiation of stress (accent) on the ultima vowel is usually perceptible: (C)V1.ˈV1(C). [p. 47] || In western dialects words having the shape #(C)V1.V1(C)# are disyllabic. In such words #(C)V1 is the penult; V1(C)# is the ultima and as such is the tonic syllable. It receives the word-accent. [p. 39] || Because word stress falls on the final syllable in Bidayuh citation forms, and perhaps in context, a clitic receives the stress placement in the word to which it is attached. [p. 94 n. 79] || They consistently accent the final syllable of the stem; this is especially evident in utterance-final position. [Part III, p. 292] || Bidayuh stems are typically disyllabic. Stress falls on the ultima of the Bidayuh word, at least in isolation. [Rensch 2006: 2]

sweep_summary: Bau-Jagoi Bidayuh (baub1235) is not in the catalog. The two bibliography items are one work: Rensch, 'Rhythm in Bidayuh', 10-ICAL 2006 preprint = SPLC 19:84-91 (2008). The 2006 PDF (and its abstract) were downloaded open from sil-philippines-languages. the SPLC print copy itself was not located (sil.org blocks downloads, no archived copy at the Internet Archive) but is the same paper. The paper is chiefly about vowel-duration rhythm (lengthened ultima vowels; full vs reduced penult vowels, absent in Western dialects), and it states word stress directly: 'Stress falls on the ultima of the Bidayuh word, at least in isolation' (§2, p. 2), with a Western-specific note that rearticulated V.V sequences carry the stress onset on the final vowel (fn 3). The fuller first-hand statement is Rensch et al. 2012 (SIL e-Book 33, already held by the project from the buka1257 search), §4.1.2 p. 47 and §3.3.2 p. 39, which names the western dialects (Singai, Jagoi) and says the ultima is the tonic syllable receiving the word accent, (C)V1.ˈV1(C); fn 79 p. 94 and §6.2.4 p. 292 repeat final stress (citation forms; utterance-final). Reading: fixed final word stress, non-contrastive, no length/tone in Western Bidayuh; a catalog record for baub1235 could be built on these two Rensch sources. Nothing remains to acquire (priority none for both items).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary word stress falls on the last syllable (the ultima) of the word/stem in citation forms; this holds across the Bidayuh dialect network and is stated explicitly for the western (Singai, Jagoi = Bau-Jagoi) dialects, where even rearticulated same-vowel sequences (C)V1.V1(C) are two syllables with the accent on the final one. Stems are typically disyllabic; the penult never carries the peak.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any examined source.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for placement. Word-final glides: stress 'falls on the first (more syllabic) of the two' vocoids, i.e. still the final syllable (p. 37). In Western (Bau-Jagoi) dialects rearticulated (C)V1.V1(C) words are disyllabic with the second (final) vowel stressed (p. 39, p. 47). The full/reduced penult-vowel contrast of eastern/central dialects does not operate in western dialects (p. 39; Rensch 2006 Pattern D), so no penult prominence contrast in Bau-Jagoi.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms: 'at least in citation forms (words that are pronounced individually)' (p. 47); Rensch 2006 p. 2: 'at least in isolation'; Part III p. 292 adds that final-syllable accent is 'especially evident in utterance-final position'; p. 94 n.79: 'perhaps in context'. Post-clitics attached to a word take the stress (p. 94 n.79). No instrumental data.
new_statements.identity_note: The deciding source treats 'Bidayuh' as a network of ~25 dialects in four clusters; Bau-Jagoi Bidayuh [sne] = Rensch's 'Western Bidayuh (Singai-Jagoi)' cluster (Singai, Jagoi, Serambu, Gumbang, Bratak, Krokong; Bau District). The p. 47 statement is pan-Bidayuh but is immediately followed by a western-dialect (Singai, Jagoi) specific stress remark, and §3.3.2 p. 39 is explicitly about western dialects; Rensch 2006 includes Serambu/Singai/Gumbang data. Not a description of one village dialect. Hliboi (Smith 2021, West Kalimantan) is only tentatively assigned to sne by Glottolog's bibliography.

new_statements.reading: Fixed final (ultima) word stress in all Bidayuh dialects, stated explicitly for the western (Singai, Jagoi = Bau-Jagoi) dialects: the ultima is the tonic syllable and carries the word accent, even when penult and ultima have the same vowel (CV1.ˈV1C); stress is non-contrastive; enclitics take the stress as the new final syllable; the 'at least in citation forms / especially utterance-final' hedge means connected-speech placement was not separately verified. Candidate catalog's classification for baub1235: fixed final, domain word (citation forms), lexical_stress no, no phonemic length in Western Bidayuh (rearticulated vowels instead), no tone. Rensch 2006/2008 §2 p. 2 gives the same rule in one sentence and is the title-search the deciding source.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (rule 01 / 001 / 0001..: fixed final) and as both existing statements, which were already taken from this Part II (pp. 39 and 47). The 2006 SIL archive entry is marked 'Availability: Not Available Online', so the print first edition itself was not opened; the 2012 SIL e-Book 33 edition held by the project is the same Part II by the same author (preface p. xi: 'some points of analysis in Part II have been modified' since 2006), so the 2006 wording could differ in detail but the stress rule is unlikely to have changed. Part III (Calvin R. Rensch) independently corroborates: p. 131 'All of them occur in the final (stressed) syllable of words'; p. 292 'They…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress (the 'word-accent', the 'tonic syllable') falls on the ultima, the last syllable of the word, in every Bidayuh dialect, stated explicitly for the western dialects (Singai, Jagoi): even in disyllables where penult and ultima carry the same vowel, (C)V1.ˈV1(C), the ultima is the tonic syllable. Stress is positional, not contrastive. The hedge 'at least in citation forms' (and n. 79 'in Bidayuh citation forms, and perhaps in context') means the author verified placement in words pronounced in isolation, not in connected speech.
new_statements.exceptions: (a) Word-final [Vi]/[Vu] sequences are analysed as vowel + semivowel partly because 'stress falls on the first (more syllabic) of the two rather than on the second' (p. 37), so the phonetic final vocoid is not a separate stressed syllable. (b) Post-clitics: 'Because word stress falls on the final syllable in Bidayuh citation forms, and perhaps in context, a clitic receives the stress placement in the word to which it is attached' (n. 79, p. 94), i.e. the stress moves to the clitic as the new final syllable. (c) Western dialects have no vowel-length contrast in the ultima (rearticulated vowels instead), so no weight sensitivity is at issue.
new_statements.identity_note: Rensch's Part II covers all four Bidayuh dialect clusters (SIL subject languages bth Biatah, sdo Bukar-Sadung, sne Bau, trx Tringgus-Sembaan); the stress statements at pp. 39 and 47 name the 'western dialects (Singai, Jagoi)' explicitly, which are the Bau-Jagoi / sne varieties that baub1235 covers, so the rule is stated for this glottocode's dialects and not only for Bidayuh in general. Bongarrá de Vega 2006 is on Singai, a western (Bau district) variety, so it would have been about this glottocode had it opened.

sources.quote: Bidayuh stems are typically disyllabic. Stress falls on the ultima of the Bidayuh word, at least in isolation. [...] In Western Bidayuh vowels may be rearticulated, i.e., there are sequences of identical (or diverse) vowels with the onset of the second vowel marked by an articulatory pulse coinciding with the onset of stress. For example, Gumbang (Western) [ . ] 'ironwood', [ . ] 'itchy'. These are sequences of vowels that form the nucleus of successive syllables. Western Bidayuh does not have lengthened vowels in the usual sense.
